To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
irradiation-induced lesions of the granule cells of the fascia dentata of the hippocampus in neonatal rats produce spontaneous perseverative turning, which is not present in normal animals.

radiation-induced damage to the dentate gyrus of the neonatal hippocampus causes spontaneous perseverative turning in adult rats, and that spontaneous bowl turning can serve as a measure of spontaneous alternation and as a sensitive indicator of radiation-induced damage to neonatal hippocampus.

radiation-induced damage to the neonatal rat hippocampal formation causes rats to turn in long, unbroken bouts without reversals when placed in a circular arena, to perseverate on the same arm of a T-ma ze when placed there to explore spontaneously, to be retarded in learning a passive avoidance task when tested with a discrete-trial procedure, and to show a high level of horizontal locomotion in an activity chamber.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of radiation-induced hippocampus damage on behavior and with the effects of hippocampal stimulation on behavior.
the development of behavioral methods to assess hippocampal function in rats.
the effects of radiation on behavior and the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
radiation damage to the hippocampus causes perseverative behavior.
radiation-induced damage to the granule cell layers of the hippocampi of rats produces spontaneous perseverative turning and other behaviors characteristic of lesions specific to this region.
the hippocampus is involved in the regulation of the speed and accuracy of movement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the radiation model of hippocampal lesions is a useful tool for studying the role of the hippocampus in memory and learning, and that the model has been used to study the effects of radiation-induced hippocampus lesions on learning and memory in the rat.
the radiation damage to neonatal rat brain is a useful model of the behavioral effects of damage to the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus.
the radiation-induced damage of the dentate gyrus is the cause of the perseverative behaviors in the T-maze and the spontaneous bowl turning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
radiation-induced damage to the fascia dentata causes rats to spontaneously turn in bowls in long, slow, perseverative bouts.
radiation-induced damage to the dentate gyrus of the neonatal brain can produce behavioral deficits in adulthood.
spontaneous turning in rats is a useful measure of hippocampal function and that radiation can be used to produce hippocampal lesions in rats.
